articles.expand: Bullock’s comment pushes back modestly against market pricing that has all but ruled out a December hike. It could offer the Australian dollar some support after it fell this week to its lowest level since late January. One line on a panel is unlikely to shift pricing on its own, so the minutes are the bigger test. Any sign that the majority on the board saw a real chance of further tightening would firm up the hawkish reading of Bullock’s remarks. If the minutes play up how close the vote was, front-end rates may decide the governor’s comment is a hedge, not a signal. - Minutes preview here: ...

articles.title: Tiff Macklem should have been fired, not celebrated
articles.expand: Tiff Macklem announced that he will retire after his seven-year term ends in June 2027. He should have left much sooner. It continues to baffle me that no central banker paid the price for the disastrous covid inflation. In no other high-profile field in the world is incompetence tolerated to the extent it is in central banking. It's a field that's protected both by government independence and a culture that accepts failure. No one exemplified that more than Tiff Macklem and his performance during the pandemic. articles.expand: Takata’s speech is the clearest public argument yet for a faster BOJ hiking pace than markets assume. He rejects a fixed quarterly rhythm and argues for reaching the middle of the neutral range early, which puts a move beyond 1.5% within view. Because his views are his own and he has been outvoted, it doesn’t change December pricing by itself. But it supports the yen and adds upward pressure on front-end JGB yields, especially with USD/JPY near 160. articles.expand: Knot’s line on fiscal discipline matters most for euro zone sovereign spreads, especially French bonds against German Bunds. A president with that view could make investors less willing to bet on a full central bank backstop if French finances get worse, which risks wider spreads during periods of stress. articles.expand: An explicit signal from the Bundesbank president that further tightening is likely should support the euro and push up short-dated euro zone yields, especially German two-year debt. Because he ties the risk directly to gas and electricity, euro zone rate pricing is now more sensitive to moves in energy markets, so a rise in oil or gas could feed quickly into ECB hike expectations.
